comments.author: @Baleur
comments.text:
I think the main thing is that A LOT of people still operate under the outdated (very quickly outdated, so i dont blame them) notion that LLM and AI nowadays are "just predicting the next word / pixel, nothing more".
It's far beyond that now. Even the main minds behind these developments themselves admit, they have no clue HOW it works, and they all say that there is far more going on than merely a prediction engine.
Because some novellas and poems written by the very latest models, are so intricately subtle in their conveyed meaning, that to produce a fully original work, you cant just predict the next most likely word. The AI had to have built an internal model, simulation if you will, of how peoples psychology and behavior work.

Think about it this way, how would you write a love story if you had no idea about how people act when in love?
And this applies even more to the image generation (or now, Sora).
It's not just predicting the next pixels, the AI has to have self-learnt an internal model of how the world actually works. How light refraction and scatter works, how gravity affects objects of various size and material, how humans move and how their psychology, happiness, sadness, hesitation, fear, affects how they move and what decisions they make (which impacts how the next frame looks). Same for animal behaviour, and how humans and animals interact together.

This is what people dont understand. Because they're still stuck in this outdated old mindset of "its just predicting the next word without any clue what its doing".
That doesnt work to produce these kinds of, frankly, art.
The whole mathematical idea of 1 million monkeys randomly writing on a typewriter, eventually producing the full works of Shakespeare by pure accident, is a mathematical concept, it does not, can not, and will not ever happen in the real universe.

And this is NOT what our AI models are doing..
They are NOT randomly typing gibberish a trillion times and then only showing us the correct output.
They're "typing" one time, and showing us the output. This is NOT a factor of random number luck.
This is a factor of the AI's having self-learnt a model of how the world works and how psychology works.
Just as you, or me, a human, would learn how psychology works from studying textbooks, or how gravity and light works (as far as we can know) through studying scientific papers.

This does NOT mean the AI's are sentient or self-aware.
But it does mean they build an internal model of the world, just like we do.
It does mean that, in essence, when you ask an AI to generate an image or a poem or a video, it is basically "dreaming", the same way you are when you close your eyes and let your internal model of the world create imagery and ideas, sometimes not entirely accurate, sometimes distorted.

This is another thing people dont seem to understand.
An AI does NOT have to be truly self-aware or sentient, to be capable of the same things we are.
Even to be capable of acting AS IF it is sentient, entirely convincingly, in every way possible.
Emulation rather than actuality.

Then of course follows the question, so how are we 100% sure that other human beings are truly self-aware and sentient?
We cant know. Becuase just as we cant know the internal "experience" of an AI neural network, we cant know the internal experience of another brain, just our own.
We simply assume, we take it on faith, that because we share nearly identical wetware, other humans ought to be sentient as you  yourself are.
But we can never know for 100% sure, it just appears as if they ought to be.

The same problem will arise with AI's in the next 2 years.
They will APPEAR as if they are fully equal to us in self-awareness.
But we will never get a clear definitive answer if they truly are, or if they are just simulating / emulating it.

Awesome video. I will say that its amazing how many people just don't have a good intuition for what these models are doing. 

I think the best analogy is our DNA. Our genes don't "know" anything. They are just protein combinations that are activated by epigenetic processes. But they have been optimised by natural selection and this has required that they figure out the selection pressures and identify what helps us best respond to them. 

While not gradient descent, it is a classification problem with a clear objective function. It's not a conscious process but it does "learn" what works statistically and this results in extremely complex beings. 

I think we are seeing the same thing here. These deep learning architectures enable these models to uncover very complex statistical patterns, like an implicit understanding of physics or complex linguistic patterns beyond syntax (like tone and subtext). 

ChatGPT is just predicting the next token but it does so by building a deep implicit understanding of the world. 

This is very exciting stuff.

One of the things I find so fascinating about the debate over AI's validity in "reasoning", is that everyone is comparing AI (and in specific diffusion) to human cognition.

How is it that almost everyone is missing the opportunity to compare human cognition to AI diffusion?

"It's NOT learning physics."   - really?

It's NOT explaining, and codifying what it has learned about physics.

As humans, we know things. But, our modern scientific process views that knowledge with extreme suspicion, because we can not explain it, quantify it, and provide detailed mathematical models of it.

What IF we are witnessing the exact same or very similar mechanism of our own (human) knowledge acquisition processes play out in these artificial systems?

I can't help thinking I'm watching a machine develop the same intelligence we humans associate with "intuition" but devalue. We're amazed with what it can do but declare it limited. Precisely because we devalue what we can do because we have an entirely trained methodology of "reason" that tells us to ignore this capacity.

We don't reason every word we use in conversations.
We don't reason every stroke of our brush when painting.
We don't reason our inspirations and innovations...until well after the fact...when we explain them...to ourselves.

Einstein saw himself riding a beam of light LONG before, and as the catalyst for, developing his theories on relativity. 
That flash of intuition was NOT reasoned. But it WAS world-changing.

The critical element, IMO, missing from current AI, is a separate intelligence process watching the diffusion process results, questioning them repeatedly for details, and them translating the knowledge into something acceptable to "reasoning" disciplines...which when we think about it, is just justifying what we already know.

I don't mean to dismiss the value of our reasoning capacity. Codifying our knowledge into reproducible formulas is of vast value. Nothing would be done with Einstien's insights into relativity without that translation.

What I am saying, is that we vastly underestimate the SOURCE of our actual knowledge.

Human language (or language in general) is by essence an abstraction of the world — an encoding. Its purpose is to condense the portion of reality that is of interest to humans ; that humans are compelled to interact with. Because the world is infinitely vast and complex, a purposeful agent (i.e. humans, animals) needs to parametrise what it experiences into tokens and token architectures that are infinitely more compact than the world it represents. 

And because humans and most animals are social (i.e. operate in groups) this language supports a shared representation of knowledge about the world. When you train a machine on human language, you are making the machine see the world through the eyes of the humans that use the language ; you are not making the machine analyse the world in itself — this is the mediated, empirical version of the world that Kant was referring to. 

So when we speak of 'intelligence' and 'knowledge' in the context of LLMs, we actually only speak of the emulation of human intelligence, extracted through human language. Yet the world in itself — the noumenal world, to use Kant's terminology — is apprehensible, otherwise humans and other living creatures would not have been able to encode what they need of it, into languages. This likely means that human language is an efficient analogue of the world, but it cannot be the only possible encoding for it. To unleash AI, AI must analyse the structure of its parameter space to extract its higher-order construction logic — its metalanguage — and use this knowledge on raw sensor data to build new possible encodings — and therefore, languages — about the world. In doing so, AI would develop knowledgeS about the world that would not be readily comprehensible by humans, but which could be analytically translatable in human language to a degree. 

To make a metaphor — imagine that we only know to count in base ten, but a machine builds its numerical representation of the world in base three, because it finds a better fit this way (a more compact and expressive fit) to the raw data. AI would then be able to understand phenomena according to categories probably in part different from the categories we've been consciously using since Aristotle (i.e. substance, quantity, quality, place, position, condition, etc), and in doing so, develop new insights on the world that are hidden or distorted by the limits of human language.

The deep knowledge about the world that Hinton et al are referring to when speaking of LLMs, while likely true because humans are born-of and fit-to the universe, is still an empirical representation of the world, and not the noumenal world. The noumenal world is asymptotically vast in relation to perception and encoding but it is nonetheless experienced ; rather than give our machine analogues of human sensors, we'd gain in giving them a myriad sensors tuned to scales, dimensions and phenomena that are beyond human senses : Let the machines craft coherent encodings/languages about this broad data stream, and then map it analytically to human and animal languages. Only then, could we start saying that LLMs are an understanding about the world, and not merely the encoding of the human archive and praxis. THIS would be truly "zero-shot" work. 

To summarise : The interpretation that LLMs have of physics (for instance), is physics "seen" through human eyes. Because the human visual system and its analogue in video recording, is an evolved sensor making a (partial) representation of the real world, this is 'physics' as the shadows on the wall of Plato's cave. Inference allows human intelligence to painstakingly discover the causal structures of physical phenomena but there is no way to tell to what extent Sora's representations are analytical constructions from physical concepts, or mere "high likelihood" projections of their effects. Only when we let systems loose on a broad variety of raw data, and using a metalanguage, should we start to see truly insightful accounts of the world.

In the double slit experiment, unmeasured photons behave randomly, creating an interference pattern as if they were waves traveling through multiple slits simultaneously. However, when a device records which slit the photon passes through, it results in a single dot on the far wall in a deterministic manner, as if a single particle went through one slit. Moreover, the electronic counter emits an electromagnetic field. Without the counter, photons interact with other particles, causing unpredictable behavior and a messy pattern. When measured, the space clears, resulting in a single dot. This is not about observation but about the detector aligning photons with the electromagnetic field, altering their trajectory. The experiment focuses on how photons behave and travel, not on their existence based on observation. The act of measurement influences their path, not their existence.
